\chapter{Estoy Hablando --- The Payoff}
\label{ch:estoy-hablando}
\hlchaptermodality{238}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can say what I am doing right now.}

I can say what I am doing right now.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[estoy hablando]{estoy hablando — the payoff}

\label{lesson:ES-C62-estoy-hablando}



\begin{quote}
\emph{Estar}, all the way through: \emph{estoy}, \emph{estás}, \emph{está}, \emph{estamos}, \emph{están}.

And one gerund. Put them side by side.
\end{quote}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: standing in the middle of doing}]
\begin{quote}
\emph{\textbf{Estoy hablando.}} — I am speaking, right now.
\end{quote}

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{} & \textbf{} \\
\midrule
\emph{Estoy} \emph{\textbf{comiendo}}. & I'm eating \\
\emph{Está} \emph{\textbf{trabajando}}. & he's working \\
\emph{Estamos} \emph{\textbf{estudiando}}. & we're studying \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

Only \emph{estar} changes. The gerund sits there, the same shape for everybody, which is why the whole construction costs you one verb you already knew and one ending.
\end{grammarlens}

\begin{culture}
It had to be \emph{estar} rather than \emph{ser}, and you already know why. \emph{Estar} is the verb for how something \textbf{temporarily stands}. An action caught mid-stride is as temporary as things get.

Now the difference from English, and it is worth having straight. English uses \emph{I'm} + \emph{-ing} for the \textbf{future} all the time: \emph{I'm eating with her tomorrow}. Spanish will not.

\begin{quote}
\emph{Estoy comiendo} — I am eating, \textbf{at this moment}, food in hand.
\end{quote}

For tomorrow, Spanish reaches for the form you learned at chapter 49: \emph{voy a comer}. So the two languages look identical here and are not: the Spanish progressive means \emph{now}, and only \emph{now}.
\end{culture}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Estoy hablando}, \emph{Estoy comiendo}
  \item \emph{Estoy comiendo} for now, then \emph{Voy a comer} for tomorrow
\end{itemize}

\emph{Twice through:}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Which verb carries the person — \emph{estar} or the gerund? (\emph{\textbf{Estar}}.)

And what can the Spanish progressive \textbf{not} do that the English one can? (Talk about the \textbf{future}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
